content.text: Chapter Nine
The Cage of Light
At dawn, Tempest Keep had lost the merciful distance that made it beautiful.

Its pale towers filled the eastern sky above Netherstorm, each curved surface bright against the violet dark. Bridges hung between the fortress and its lesser satellites without chains or visible supports. Blue fire moved through channels along their undersides. The storm below answered in slow flashes, revealing rock fragments adrift beneath the host as if the broken world were still deciding where to fall.

Falanaras watched from the forward assembly trench while Daric tightened the last strap on his shield. Around them, spellbreakers checked the emerald crystals set into their polearms and blades. Magisters moved down the line with baskets of mana stones, placing one in each waiting hand. No one called the ration generous. No one refused it.

Falanaras closed his hand around the mana stone and drew. Cold spread through his palm and climbed his arm as the crystal dimmed. Relief followed almost at once: the ache behind his eyes eased, his fingers steadied, and the fortress sharpened until he could distinguish moving defenders along the nearest bridge. The ration was enough for the advance and perhaps the first breach. Beyond that, enemy magic and discipline would have to carry them.
Daric rolled one shoulder beneath his dark plate. “I preferred the ship.”
“You spent half the voyage insulting it.”
“It never hung over a bottomless storm and invited me to walk across.” Daric looked toward the luminous span ahead. “A quality I failed to appreciate.”

The men nearest them laughed quietly. The sound did what Falanaras could not have managed with another inspection. Backs loosened. A soldier whose breathing had grown too quick forced it down into the cadence they had practiced. Falanaras met Daric’s eye and received the barest shrug.

Across the trench, Astalor’s restraint pylons stood on six low sledges. Their crimson bands were dark for now, the metal forks nested inward around hollow centers. Selorien passed among the teams with a ledger in one hand and a wrench in the other, correcting harness lengths and marking each change. Astalor inspected a hairline fracture in one focusing crystal, discarded it, and selected another without looking toward the fortress.

Liadrin waited beside the first sledge in blackened plate. She carried no priest’s staff, only a sword and a round shield scarred from Blade’s Edge. The coming encounter with living Light showed nowhere in her posture. Her stillness had the effort of a barricade built before anyone else knew an attack was coming.

Rommath crossed the assembly ground without an escort. Officers stepped toward him with reports; he answered each before they finished bowing. A failed western relay received two reserve crystals. A healer requesting more carriers received six soldiers from the prince’s household guard. When a magister warned that the storm cover might end before the second engine reached position, Rommath looked once at the fortress and ordered the engine crews forward early.
“The western crews will be exposed,” the magister said.
“Then Althene will screen them,” Rommath replied. “If the conduits remain intact, every company will be exposed.”

There was no speech before the advance. Kael’thas emerged onto the command rise in a sweep of crimson, the three Verdant Spheres burning above him. He raised one hand. Along the broken plateau, hundreds of blood elves became silent. Falanaras felt the scale of the army then: soldiers from a wounded kingdom standing beneath an alien sky, ready to spend lives on the chance that those left at home might someday stop measuring survival in mouthfuls of magic.
The prince closed his fist.
Solarian tore open the storm.

A lance of starfire descended through the cloud bank and struck the first outer conduit. The impact turned the horizon white. Siege engines answered from three ridges, hurling coils of red arcane force across the void. The fortress shields flared blue, vast and translucent, and the first barrage spread over them in burning veins.

Sanguinar’s infantry moved south in ordered ranks, shields high beneath answering bolts from the Keep. On the western heights, Althene’s rangers vanished into violet dust as if the landscape had taken them. Thaladred led the central force toward a narrow bridge of pale metal while engineers dragged the first breach engine behind him.
Falanaras drew his spellbreaker’s glaive. The metal beneath his boots had begun to hum.
“Inner approach,” he called. “Stay with the pylons until I release you. Wards before defenders. If the bridge fails, trust the anchor lines and keep your hands off the storm.”
Daric lifted his shield. “You heard the captain. We have crossed too much ground to become weather.”
They advanced beneath a sky crowded with power.
The first defender reached them halfway across the bridge.

It came over the rail in a rush of blue metal and crystal, a construct with four bladed limbs turning around a bright core. Daric caught the descending strike on his shield. The impact drove him to one knee. Falanaras cut across the construct’s center, felt an answering ward turn his blade, and reversed before the second pair of limbs could close around him.
The ward was elegant. It moved the force of his blow into the bridge instead of resisting it. Pale light rippled beneath his boots, carrying the impact toward the pylons that held the span aloft.

Falanaras turned the inner hook of his glaive across the pale current. The ward caught there as though it had found another path. Beneath its reflex he found a simpler command bound into the made creature: defend the bridge, answer the nearest hostile force. He closed his will around that purpose and changed what the construct recognized. Its blades stuttered, then turned away from Daric. When more constructs dropped from beneath the rail, the seized guardian met them in a collision of blue metal. Two went over the edge together. The command tore loose before Falanaras could preserve it. Daric rose under the first construct’s failing weight and drove the shield rim into its crystal core. Two soldiers struck with him. Blue fragments streamed away into the storm.

The surviving constructs regrouped beneath the bridge. Behind them came armored draenei, tall figures in pale plate whose crystal-headed weapons shone with the same blue-white power running through the Keep. They formed around the nearest support arch rather than charging. The first rank planted shields. The second raised glowing staves.
“Ward front,” Falanaras warned.

The draenei released their spell. A wall of force swept along the span, bright enough to erase armor and faces. Falanaras set his glaive’s point against the bridge and opened every ward fixed into his armor. The spell struck. Its command pressed for flesh and found the spellbreakers armored against its hold; heat entered their bones, but the force could not impose its full effect. Behind them, infantry, haulers, and magisters drew disciplined measures from the loose radiance, thinning the attack while the spellbreakers’ runed armor and weapons denied the remaining pressure a full purchase. The ward crystals at Falanaras’s shoulders screamed under what remained.
He could not hold it. Holding had never been the work.
“Break left!”

At his signal, the spellbreakers turned their glaives left. The runes along their armor and weapons continued denying the wall its full hold while the whole file changed angle beneath it. They did not steal the spell. They gave its remaining physical force a slanted surface and a weaker path. The blue pressure skidded west across the hooked blades and swept into the draenei’s own outer rank, casting shields, staves, and armored bodies against the rail. Daric’s infantry surged through the cleared center. Shield met shield. The bridge filled with the blunt violence of close ranks: metal battering plate, boots slipping in blood, blades finding the seams beneath arms.

A draenei defender struck down one of the pylon haulers and turned toward the exposed sledge. Liadrin intercepted him. Her shield took the crystal hammer high; her sword entered beneath his breastplate. She wrenched it free, caught the falling harness before it slid from the bridge, and thrust it into another soldier’s hands.
“The burden moves,” she said. “So do you.”
The soldier seized the straps. Liadrin moved on before gratitude could slow either of them.

A green signal burst over the western satellite. Althene’s rangers had taken the first firing platform. Their arrows began crossing the central span, black lines against the fortress glow. One struck a draenei caster through the wrist. Another shattered the focus above him. The remaining ward collapsed, and Thaladred’s forward infantry drove the defenders back beneath the outer arch.
Then the Keep answered through the bridge itself.

The pale metal split along a line beneath the third sledge. One hauler disappeared before he could cry out. The sledge tipped after him, its restraint fork grinding across the deck. Selorien threw himself onto the rear brace and caught it with both arms. The harness snapped taut around his waist.

Falanaras reached him with Daric. Together they dragged the pylon back while the gap widened under their boots. Astalor took in the missing hauler, the harness cutting into Selorien’s waist, and the blue power pulsing through the exposed interior. He ordered the remaining crews off the fractured section, then knelt at the edge.
“The support current cycles through four pulses,” Astalor said, his voice quiet and level. “The third can be suppressed. That will open an interval.”
Selorien watched the luminous channels, still gasping against the harness. “Confirmed. The next interval will reach the western fork.”

“Good.” Astalor drove a copper probe between two luminous channels. “Captain, suppress the third pulse. Magister Dawnmark, reverse the pylon on my mark. We will support the bridge long enough to clear our people.”

They obeyed. Falanaras caught the rising current and crushed it flat. Selorien forced power through the restraint pylon in the wrong direction. Astalor turned the probe. Crimson force entered the bridge’s wounded support and held the split closed long enough for the remaining sledges and soldiers to cross.
The bridge collapsed behind them.

For several heartbeats, Falanaras heard only the long metallic groan of the span falling into Netherstorm. Then the outer doors opened under Thaladred’s assault, and the army poured into Tempest Keep.
Inside, the fortress resisted them with light.

It ran through walls without lamps, gathered beneath each arch, and moved in quiet patterns across the floor. There was no soot, no dust, no stale air from sealed rooms. Tempest Keep felt awake. Every surface carried the presence of its makers, and the blood elves entered it trailing smoke, blood, and the sharp green scent of fel-fed armor.

The central force divided at the first junction. Thaladred drove east toward the defensive nexus. Sanguinar’s companies struck upward to keep the remaining garrison from concentrating around the shrine. Falanaras followed Liadrin and Astalor into a descending corridor with Daric’s infantry, Selorien’s magisters, and four surviving restraint pylons.

The loss of two pylons did not shake Astalor’s certainty that elven magic could master the task. It made him more deliberate about the danger. He redistributed the remaining emitters into a square configuration, then removed three safety limiters from their focusing crowns while Selorien recorded each alteration.
“Four emitters will form the square,” Selorien said after checking Astalor’s revised scheme. “There will be no reserve if the field recoils.”
“The original limits would deny us the strength to contain our objective,” Astalor replied. “We will accept the greater discharge.”
“The open sides of the crowns will take it first.”

Astalor glanced at the scorched leather around Selorien’s waist and nodded. “Then no one will stand there. Mark each convergence, keep the crews behind the housings, and repeat the warning before every activation.”

Selorien marked the page and raised his voice to the haulers. “You heard the magister. When the crowns open, remain behind the red housing. If a pylon turns, move with the housing and do not cross its open side.”

The corridor bent inward. The noise of the larger battle faded behind layers of sealed crystal. Falanaras began to hear another sound beneath the alarms: a low sequence of tones, too measured for machinery and too resonant for any instrument he knew. Each note settled in his chest. The ache left by the morning ration stirred, then quieted as if listening.
Liadrin heard it. Her next step shortened before discipline restored it.

A white barrier dropped across the passage. Astalor’s forward magister touched it and screamed. Fire climbed his arm beneath the skin. Liadrin seized the back of his harness and pulled him clear while Falanaras caught the barrier’s outer edge with his blade. The magic was unlike the construct wards. It did not redirect force. It entered whatever touched it and demanded an answer from the will inside.

For one searing instant he remembered Edric at the ruined way station, gold radiance held around wounded bodies while the Scourge pressed in. He remembered Liadrin among Silvermoon’s refugees, spending strength on strangers because faith had once made that use seem inevitable.
The barrier found no such faith in him. It found duty, hunger, grief, and a refusal to release the weapon in his hand.
“Now,” Rommath said behind him.

The Grand Magister’s spell entered through the weaknesses Falanaras held open. Red and gold light spread across the white barrier in branching fractures. Rommath did not attempt to understand the defense on its own terms. He fed power into every exposed fault until the working burst inward and left both of them smoking at the threshold.
Rommath stepped over the ruined line. Blood ran from one nostril. “The reserve has secured the upper junction. We have one hour before the fortress redirects enough power to isolate this wing.”
“The wounded need evacuation,” Liadrin said. The burned magister lay breathing in shallow jerks at her feet. Two soldiers had already lifted him onto a shield.
“The western route remains open.” Rommath looked at the men carrying the shield. “Take everyone who cannot fight. Return with no one. Your work is to bring them out.”
It was an order to retreat and an order to save lives, given in the same hard tone he used for ammunition. The carriers turned back. Rommath faced the inner corridor.
“Silvermoon has buried enough people while waiting for power to arrive by grace,” he said. “Move.”
They moved.

The next defenders fought to delay rather than kill. Small groups withdrew behind seals, forcing Falanaras to spend strength breaking each one while constructs struck from wall recesses and vanished before Daric could pin them. Time became another enemy. Every pause meant the fortress gathering itself around the central wing.

At the final junction, draenei vindicators held a circular stair beneath an arch of living crystal. There were fewer than twenty. Their armor was broken, and several bled through bandages tied in haste. They had chosen the place where numbers mattered least.
One called to the blood elves in accented Common. “Leave this chamber.”

No one answered. Falanaras saw the vindicator understand before the charge began. These invaders had crossed a dying world, a sea, half a continent, and the Dark Portal for what lay behind him. A warning could not send them home.

The stair became a crush of shields and radiant weapons. Daric took the center. Around him, blood elf soldiers drew measured currents from the gold strengthening draenei armor, limbs, and crystal blades, dulling each advantage through ordinary sin’dorei practice before closing with its bearer. The spellbreakers worked differently. Thrown glaives cut vindicators and caster-defenders through arm or thigh; power tore out after the blades, and the sudden loss burned through flesh from within. Others hooked completed weapon enchantments away and sent them across the line. Gold hardened Daric’s shield arm. A stolen edge of radiance settled along Liadrin’s sword. Falanaras stayed half a pace behind Daric’s right shoulder, read the most intricate working, and stripped the force from a crystal spear aimed at Daric’s throat. He took only enough loose warmth to steady his numb shoulder, then sent the intact strengthening effect into his glaive. The charged crescent broke the spear.

Liadrin fought on the left. A vindicator’s hammer split her shield and drove her against the rail. She abandoned the wreckage, caught his next swing on the strong of her blade, and stepped inside his reach. When he fell, she took the hammer in her free hand and used it to shatter the crystal brace protecting the stair’s final seal.

Daric’s shield buckled. Falanaras’s left shoulder went numb beneath a glancing blow. Selorien lost two magisters to a burst of white fire and dragged a third behind the pylon housing himself. Astalor remained crouched at the seal, his calm attention fixed on the Light moving through it while violence closed around him.
“The seal is reading intent as well as power,” Astalor said, his soft voice carrying through the clash of weapons.
Selorien parried a blade with his staff. “The response confirms it. Force alone will keep the way closed.”
Astalor glanced toward Liadrin. “Then we will not force it. The seal recognizes the Light. Give it what it was made to welcome.”
Liadrin stared at the crystal arch. The tones beyond it had grown strong enough to tremble through the rail beneath her hand.
“I have none to give it,” she said.

The last vindicator lunged for her. A completed holy enchantment wrapped his crystal weapon, lending the strike a radiance the arch recognized. Falanaras caught that working on the hook of his glaive and peeled it from the hammer before it landed. He did not disperse it. He reassigned the stolen Light to the crystal doors. Gold entered the arch in branching veins.
The doors opened.
The shrine contained no throne.

It was a round chamber open through its center to the storm below. Slender arches leaned inward without meeting, their crystal surfaces filled with slow-moving constellations. At the far side, a platform floated over the open shaft. White-gold radiance filled the air above it.
M’uru turned toward them.

Falanaras had expected a creature wearing Light as armor. The naaru had no flesh to separate from its power. Faceted limbs revolved around a hollow center brighter than the sunlit glass of Silvermoon. Runes traveled along its crystalline body and vanished into the brilliance at its heart. The tones he had heard through the fortress came from M’uru without breath or instrument, immense chords reduced by distance into something his bones could endure.
Every hunger in him went still.

Relief arrived without feeding, brief and total. The emptiness left by the Sunwell seemed to recognize what stood before him. Men behind Falanaras lowered weapons by inches. One began to weep with no sound. Daric’s damaged shield slipped against the floor, and he did not correct it.

Liadrin crossed the threshold last. The Light touched her face. For a heartbeat, the woman at Falanaras’s side vanished beneath the memory of the high priestess at Silvermoon’s inner gate: hands bright over the wounded, voice hoarse from prayer, faith offered against the end of everything.
Then Liadrin’s mouth hardened. The memory belonged to him. Whatever she faced in M’uru’s radiance was her own.

No defenders waited inside. No weapon rose from the platform. M’uru watched the blood elves bring four crimson pylons into the shrine and place them around its light. Astalor stood beside the first sledge, his gaze following the great crystalline forms as they revolved. Wonder entered his face without disguise even while his apparatus encircled the being before him.
“Extraordinary,” he said softly. He inclined his head toward M’uru, then rested one hand on the control focus. “Take your positions.”

His magisters opened the restraint crowns. Curved forks unfolded toward M’uru. Crimson lines joined the pylons into a square, each one wavering where it crossed the white radiance. Selorien checked the distance twice, confirmed each position against the ledger, and directed the haulers behind the housings before reporting the square ready.

Rommath entered with Kael’thas and the surviving household guard. The prince bore a cut across one cheek. One Verdant Sphere burned lower than the others, its fire unsteady, yet triumph had made him look more like the portraits than he had in the war room.

Kael’thas stopped before the containment square. M’uru’s revolving limbs inclined toward him. A sequence of notes passed through the chamber. The prince’s expression shifted, too slight for Falanaras to name.
“Will it answer you?” Rommath asked Liadrin.
She stood close enough that white light filled the scars on her gauntlets. “It already has.”
“What did it say?” Falanaras asked.
Liadrin looked at M’uru. “Nothing I can make smaller by speaking.”
Astalor studied the four control readings, then raised his hand over the focus. “The matrix is aligned. We will begin containment.”
The crimson square rose into a cage.

Bands of force climbed around M’uru, crossed above it, and tightened. Falanaras braced for the violence Kael’thas had planned against: a burst of Holy power, shattered pylons, soldiers burned away before they understood resistance had begun.
M’uru did not strike.

The naaru descended from the floating platform and entered the restraint square. Its light passed through the first band without effort, then drew inward until the crimson line could close around it. One faceted limb turned toward a pylon and halted a finger’s breadth from the housing. The machine trembled. M’uru withdrew rather than break it.

Astalor’s hand remained above the focus. Surprise showed only in a slight narrowing of his eyes, followed by an almost reverent attention. “Remarkable,” he said softly. “The field has closed without opposition.”
Selorien checked the four readings in sequence. “Confirmed. There is no pressure against any crown.”
Astalor looked from the instruments to M’uru. “Then the naaru is permitting us to hold it.” No one contradicted him.

Beyond the shrine, the fortress alarms began to fail one by one. Each silence marked another blood elf objective secured. The campaign had succeeded. The outer conduits were broken, the defensive nexus taken, the surviving garrison divided, and the power at the center of it all stood within Astalor’s cage.

Falanaras wanted the success to feel complete. He thought of Silvermoon’s dim common rooms, of soldiers watching one another’s hands for tremors, of Rynel bowed over stolen power in Deatholme. M’uru might end that inheritance. The promise had become more credible with every step toward the shrine.
It had also watched them arrive and chosen not to stop them.
That willingness entered the victory and remained there.
They carried M’uru out through a conquered fortress.

The four pylons locked into a levitating frame around the naaru. Crimson bands held their square while white radiance spilled between them, washing blood from its color and laying bright paths across the walls. Soldiers stepped aside as the frame passed. Some bowed. Others stared with the naked concentration of the starving before a feast.

The wounded lifted their heads. One elf with a bandage wrapped across both eyes reached toward the warmth until a healer caught his wrist. M’uru’s tones moved through them all, gentle enough to make the chains around it seem harsher.

No one fed. Astalor had forbidden contact until the matrix could be tested under controlled conditions. The order traveled ahead of the procession, repeated by officers and enforced by guards. Falanaras heard disappointment sharpen into irritation along the ranks, then vanish beneath discipline.

At the broken outer arch, Althene waited with seven of the rangers who had taken the western platform. Blood had dried down one side of her neck. Her left sleeve was burned away from shoulder to wrist.
She looked past Falanaras to the cage. “That is what we came for?”
“Yes.”
Althene studied the open storm behind it, the unbroken pylons, and the blood elves escorting it with weapons drawn. “How difficult was the restraint?”
Falanaras glanced at Selorien. The magister’s ledger remained closed beneath one arm. “It came with us.”
Althene’s gaze returned to M’uru. Her expression did not change, but she asked no more questions.

The return bridge had been secured from the western satellite. Below it, wreckage from the assault turned slowly in the storm. Daric walked beside Falanaras with his ruined shield strapped across his back and one hand pressed to a cut beneath his ribs.
“You were right,” Daric said.
“About what?”
“The bridge was worse than the ship.” His eyes stayed on the white figure within the cage. “I have not decided about the rest.”
Neither had Falanaras.

The staging grounds saw the radiance before they saw the returning soldiers. Figures emerged from trenches and repair tents. Work stopped along the siege lines. When Kael’thas stepped onto the plateau behind M’uru’s frame, the first cheer began among Sanguinar’s infantry and spread across the camp.

The sound rolled over Falanaras in waves. Bloodied soldiers raised weapons. Magisters who had spent the night counting losses embraced beside their engines. Someone cried, “For Quel’Thalas,” and hundreds answered until the fractured land seemed to carry the name homeward.

Falanaras joined them. His voice broke against the last syllable. The victory was real. Men and women had died to secure it. The source within the cage might spare others from Rynel’s end, from the Wretched quarters, from years of rationed weakness and private shame. Refusing to name that hope would have been another kind of dishonesty.
M’uru made no sound above the cheering.

Later, after Astalor’s teams had anchored the cage inside the command ward and guards had cleared the curious from its perimeter, Falanaras found Liadrin standing beyond the outer line. The Light painted one side of her armor white. The other remained black against Netherstorm.
“You said it answered,” he said.
“It saw us.”
“That is not the same.”
“No.” Liadrin watched the bands pass over M’uru’s revolving limbs. “It is worse.”
The admission struck harder for its lack of defense. Falanaras had expected her severity to offer a way around what happened in the shrine. Instead she held her gaze on it.
“Then why did it come?” he asked.

“I do not know.” Her voice was low. “Perhaps it knows more of the road ahead than we do. Perhaps mercy can look like surrender when seen from the wrong end of time. Perhaps it judged us and found resistance less useful than witness.”
“We mean to imprison a living being and take its Light into ourselves.”
Liadrin turned to him. Her face held the exhaustion of the battle and something older that the shrine had uncovered. “Yes.”
“You do not hesitate.”

“I served the Light while our kingdom died,” she said. “I know what it means to profane what I once held sacred. M’uru’s power could steady our soldiers, preserve our children, and keep hunger from finishing what the Scourge began. We have chained a being who offered us no violence, and we intend to take what belongs to it. Say the wrong plainly. Then remember whom we commit it to save.”

Her answer offered no pardon and sought none. Liadrin placed the wrong beside the need without allowing either to erase the other, then moved forward under both. Falanaras understood why soldiers would follow her, even beneath the burden of what they had done. The act remained unrighteous, and responsibility became impossible to evade.

Inside the command ward, Astalor began the first containment measurements. Magisters adjusted the pylons without drawing from their captive. Kael’thas stood over the results while Rommath dispatched casualty rolls and orders for the return route. The machinery of victory resumed around the being who had permitted it.
M’uru turned within the crimson bands. White-gold light passed over Falanaras, Liadrin, the guards, and the blood drying on the ground. Its tones began again, quiet enough to hear beneath the storm.
At dawn, Falanaras had believed they were marching toward an answer.
By nightfall, the answer was marching with them.
